title: Your end-to-end design project
idea: An end-to-end low-level design (LLD) is a repeatable path: requirements, classes, lifecycles, strategies, an API with typed errors, and a run that proves each requirement.
points: Pick a chapter system or a fresh domain; this page uses library lending.
Write numbered requirements first; each later class or check should trace to one.
Model each lifecycle as an `enum` with an allowed-moves table, not scattered flags.
Put each rule likely to change behind a one-method strategy, injected through the constructor.

items.label: 1 · Clarify
items.text: List actors, use cases and limits as numbered requirements. Ask what is excluded.

items.label: 2 · Classes
items.text: Nouns become classes or records, verbs become service methods. Give each class one owner.

items.label: 3 · Lifecycles
items.text: Anything with a status gets an `enum` and an allowed-moves table.

items.label: 4 · Variation
items.text: Fines, pricing, matching: each rule that may change becomes a strategy interface.

items.label: 5 · API, errors
items.text: Name the public methods and one error code per failure, read from `code()`.

items.label: 6 · Prove it
items.text: A `main` runs the happy path and every error; checks trace to requirements.

code.title: Steps 2–5: the slice
code.caption: A thin, complete slice of library lending: model, lifecycle, swappable fine rule and typed errors.

walk.text: Steps 2 to 4 output: a state `enum`, an immutable `Loan` record and a one-method `FinePolicy` strategy.
Step 5: one unchecked exception with a stable `code()`, so callers branch on codes, not message text.
The constructor rejects bad config and receives the fine rule: dependency injection, no hidden `new`.
Guard clauses first: unknown copy and wrong state fail with different codes before any change.
Returning a copy frees it and asks the policy for the fine. The service never computes money itself.
Step 6: the same scenario runs under two policies. Only the injected lambda differs.

code.title: Step 6: requirement checks
code.caption: A tiny `check` runner turns numbered requirements into PASS or FAIL lines, no test library needed. These checks use the full four-state `CopyState` the slice grows into; the slice's `borrow` would call `canMoveTo` instead of its `if`.

walk.text: A hand-written runner: print the requirement name and count failures. Teams use JUnit 5 for this.
The full lifecycle as data: each state lists where it may go. `EnumMap` keeps it compact and ordered.
A state missing from the table yields an empty set, so it can never move, instead of crashing.
Each check names its requirement, so a reviewer sees which promise broke, not just a stack trace.
Every state needs a rule, catching a forgotten new state. Drop it if a state is truly final.
Strategies are tested alone, with no service or state around them.

pitfalls: Drawing twenty classes before listing requirements; the interviewer cannot tell which class serves what.
Using `boolean` flags like `isLent` and `isLost`; two can be true at once.
Stopping at a diagram; with no running `main`, nobody sees the errors handled.

quiz.q: Halfway through, the interviewer adds: fines are capped at 50. Which change fits this design best?
options: Write a new `FinePolicy` and inject it into `LendingService`
Add a `maxFine` field to the `Loan` record
quiz.why: Fines already vary behind `FinePolicy`. A capped policy, the smaller of 50 and the base fine, is a new class injected into `LendingService`; the service is not edited.

takeaway: Requirements in, running proof out: every class traces to a numbered need.

starters: Can you review my requirement list for a cab booking design before I draw classes?
